<reflection>
The first experiment provided kinetic data under moderate conditions, but the fitting results show that many mechanisms have very similar negative log-likelihood (NLL) values, with differences less than 0.1 for most. This indicates that the data from a single condition is insufficient to discriminate among the large set of candidate mechanisms. The top group includes M7, M6, M8, M16, M17, M12, M1, and many others, all within a narrow NLL range. Only M3, M4, and M5 are slightly worse but still within a plausible range (ΔNLL < 1). The aim of the first experiment was to establish a baseline, which was achieved, but further discrimination is needed.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To discriminate among the many plausible mechanisms, I propose an experiment with a lower catalyst concentration (0.001 M) while keeping substrate concentration at 2.0 M and no initial product. This condition probes the dependence of the kinetics on catalyst concentration, which is expected to affect mechanisms differently. For simple Michaelis-Menten (M1), the initial rate should scale linearly with catalyst concentration at low substrate saturation. Mechanisms involving dimerization (e.g., M2, M3, M13, M18, M19) will exhibit non-linear scaling because dimer formation depends on [cat]^2. Activation mechanisms (M6, M8) may show lag phases or different effective rate constants at low catalyst levels. Deactivation mechanisms (M9-M20) might become more pronounced if deactivation consumes a significant fraction of the catalyst when its total concentration is low. By comparing the progress curves from this low-catalyst condition with the previous moderate-catalyst condition, we can assess deviations from simple scaling and thus narrow down the candidate set. This design avoids extreme conditions (e.g., saturation or depletion) and targets a broad range of mechanisms simultaneously, rather than focusing on a single pair.
</hypothesis>
